entries.explanation: Roe deer; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Reh (roe deer) + Wild (game).

entries.explanation: Red deer; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Rot (red) + Wild (game).

entries.explanation: Fallow deer; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Dam (fallow deer) + Wild (game).

entries.explanation: Sika deer; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Sika (deer name of Japanese origin) + Wild (game).

entries.explanation: Mouflon; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Muffel (mouflon) + Wild (game).

entries.explanation: Chamois; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Gams (chamois) + Wild (game).

entries.explanation: Wild boar; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Schwarz (black) + Wild (game).

entries.explanation: Brown hare; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Feld (field) + Hase (hare).

entries.explanation: Rabbit; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Ordinary German for rabbit; the word came into German through older European rabbit names.

entries.explanation: Fox; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Ordinary German for fox; an inherited Germanic animal name.

entries.explanation: Badger; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Ordinary German for badger; an old Germanic animal name.

entries.explanation: Marten; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Ordinary German for marten; an inherited animal name.

entries.explanation: Raccoon; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Wasch- (washing) + Bär (bear), from its handling of food.

entries.explanation: Wildcat; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Wild (wild) + Katze (cat).

entries.explanation: Marmot; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: The traditional German marmot name, reshaped from older forms; not a transparent compound of modern words.

entries.explanation: Pheasant; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: The pheasant name was borrowed through European languages; it is not a hunting disguise word.

entries.explanation: Partridge; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: A traditional compound ending in Huhn (fowl); the first element's origin is not established here.

entries.explanation: Greylag goose; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Grau (gray) + Gans (goose).

entries.explanation: Wood pigeon; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: Ringel (ring) + Taube (pigeon).

entries.explanation: Eagle owl; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: An onomatopoeic name resembling the owl's call.

entries.explanation: Buzzard; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of game animals.
entries.etymology: The ordinary German bird name; its historical origin is not established here.

entries.explanation: Female wild boar (sow); used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: Traditional name for a female wild boar; no historical origin asserted.

entries.explanation: Male wild boar (boar); used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: Male wild boar; resemblance to Keil (wedge) is a mnemonic, not a verified derivation.

entries.explanation: Wild boar piglet; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: Related to frisch (fresh or new): young wild boar.

entries.explanation: Yearling wild boar; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: Über (over) + laufen (run); a young boar in its next year.

entries.explanation: Male deer (stag); used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: Old Germanic word for a deer or stag.

entries.explanation: Male roe deer (buck); used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: Ordinary German for buck or male goat; also a male of several game species.

entries.explanation: Female roe deer (doe); used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: Ordinary German for female goat; hunting term for a roe-deer doe.

entries.explanation: Young roe deer (fawn); used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: Young goat or fawn; a juvenile game animal.

entries.english: Antlerless female and young red deer
entries.explanation: Antlerless female and young red deer; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: Kahl (bare) + Wild (game), for antlerless red deer.

entries.explanation: Group of wild boar; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: An old word for a group or troop; a wild boar sounder.

entries.explanation: Group of roe deer; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of animal terms.
entries.etymology: Literally jump or leap; specialized term for a roe-deer group.

entries.explanation: Antlers; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: The established German word for antlers, shed and regrown by deer.

entries.explanation: Roe deer antlers; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: From Horn (horn); specialized hunting usage can refer to roe-deer antlers.

entries.explanation: Literally 'snails'; describes the curled horns of mouflon.
entries.etymology: Literally 'snails'; the curling horns of a mouflon resemble snail shells.

entries.explanation: Literally 'roses'; the rough coronets at the base of antlers.
entries.etymology: Literally roses; hunting term for antler coronets.

entries.explanation: Antler pedicle; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: Rosen (antler coronet) + Stock (stem/base).

entries.explanation: Pearling on antlers; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: Literally pearls; small bead-like antler bumps.

entries.explanation: Palmated antler sections; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: Literally shovels; broad flattened antler palms.

entries.explanation: Middle antler tine; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: Mittel (middle) + Sprosse (tine or shoot).

entries.explanation: Bez tine; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: A traditional antler-tine name; do not assume Eis (ice) gives its historical origin.

entries.explanation: Six-point antlered buck; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: Sechs (six) + -er: a six-pointed buck.

entries.explanation: Spike-antlered male; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: Spieß (spear or spike) + -er: spike-antlered male.

entries.explanation: Vestigial canine teeth of deer; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: Hunting term for red-deer canine teeth; no modern literal translation is established here.

entries.explanation: Wild boar tusks; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: Literally 'weapons'; wild boar tusks function as defensive weapons.

entries.explanation: Chamois-hair hat ornament; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of antlers and trophies.
entries.etymology: Gams (chamois) + Bart (beard).

entries.english: Blood of wounded or harvested game
entries.explanation: Literally 'sweat'; in Jägersprache it means blood from game, especially when tracking a wounded animal.
entries.etymology: Literally 'sweat'; in hunting language, blood from game, particularly a wound trail. A secret-code origin is not established.

entries.explanation: Hide of cloven-hoofed game; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: Literally 'cover' or 'blanket'; the animal's hide covers its body.

entries.explanation: Wild boar hide; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: Ordinarily a rind or thick skin; the specialized hunting word for wild boar hide.

entries.explanation: Fur-bearing animal pelt; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: An established German word for an animal skin or pelt, especially fur-bearing small game.

entries.explanation: A fox's tail; a species-specific hunting term.
entries.etymology: Literally a fuse or slow match; in hunting language a fox's tail. The resemblance is a memory aid, not proof of historical origin.

entries.explanation: Literally 'flower'; hunters use it for a rabbit's tail.
entries.etymology: Literally 'flower'; a traditional hunting term for a rabbit or hare tail.

entries.explanation: Literally 'mirror'; the pale rump patch used to identify deer.
entries.etymology: Literally 'mirror'; the conspicuous pale rump patch.

entries.explanation: Heart-lung shot area; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: Literally leaf or sheet; in hunting language the shoulder area.

entries.explanation: Location of shot impact; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: An (at) + Schuss (shot): shot site.

entries.explanation: Stationary hunting from a stand; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: An (at) + Sitz (seat): stationary hunt.

entries.explanation: Stalking hunt; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: Traditional hunting word for stalking quietly; its historical origin is not established here.

entries.explanation: Follow-up tracking of wounded game; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: Nach (after) + Suche (search): follow-up tracking.

entries.explanation: Hunting district; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: District or territory; the managed hunting area.

entries.explanation: Baiting or feeding site; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: From kirren, to attract game with feed.

entries.explanation: Game trail or passage; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: Literally change or alternation; a regular animal passage.

entries.explanation: Higher-status game category; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: Hoch (high) + Wild (game): historically privileged game.

entries.explanation: Small or lower-status game category; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: Nieder (low) + Wild (game): historically lower-status game.

entries.explanation: Blood-tracking dog; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of hunting language.
entries.etymology: Schweiß (blood in hunting language) + Hund (dog): a dog trained to track wounded game.

entries.explanation: Ethical and proper hunting conduct; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Waid (traditional hunting element) + Gerechtigkeit (rightness or justice).

entries.explanation: Traditional greeting or congratulations between hunters; the response is Waidmannsdank.
entries.etymology: Waidmann (hunter) + Heil (good fortune).

entries.english: Response of thanks to a hunter
entries.explanation: Response of thanks to a hunter; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Waidmann (hunter) + Dank (thanks).

entries.explanation: Shooter's ceremonial branch; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Schütze (shooter) + Bruch (broken branch).

entries.english: Last bite placed in game animal's mouth
entries.explanation: Literally 'last bite'; a branch placed in the mouth of male cloven-hoofed game as a mark of respect.
entries.etymology: Literally 'last bite': a ceremonial final twig.

entries.explanation: Branch marking the shot location; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Anschuss (shot site) + Bruch (branch).

entries.explanation: Warning branch; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Warn- (warning) + Bruch (branch).

entries.explanation: Ownership branch; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Inbesitznahme (taking possession) + Bruch (branch).

entries.english: Ceremonial laying out of harvested game
entries.explanation: Ceremonial laying out of harvested game; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Strecke (laid-out bag) + legen (to lay).

entries.explanation: End-of-hunt horn signal; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Traditional hunting-horn cry or signal; historical derivation is not established here.

entries.explanation: Respectful wait after a shot; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Toten (dead) + Wacht (vigil); historical hunting usage needs verification.

entries.explanation: Driven hunt; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Treiben (drive) + Jagd (hunt).

entries.explanation: King of the hunt; used in German hunting terminology and class discussions of traditions.
entries.etymology: Jagd (hunt) + König (king).

etymologyScope: Literal meaning and word structure are not proof of historical derivation. Do not present Jägersprache as uniformly originating in poachers' secret language.
